subject: Ottawa's year-end ask: lower tariffs, then CUSMA talks
bodyMarkdown:
Ottawa is trying to sign something with Washington before the year ends, and what it is trying to sign is much smaller than a new CUSMA. If you work in autos, steel, aluminum or lumber, or you hold a Canadian bank or rail stock that lends to them, the shape of that smaller thing tells you more about your 2027 than any speech about free trade.

## What Ottawa is actually asking for

CBC reported on Friday, citing sources, that the federal government wants an interim trade arrangement with the Trump administration by the end of the year. Dominic LeBlanc told CBC's Power & Politics that such an arrangement would lower **Section 232** tariffs, the sectoral duties Washington imposes on national security grounds, on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, and would remove the **Section 338** tariffs, a separate set imposed in September, entirely. LeBlanc has also said some Section 232 duties would stay, at reduced rates. So what Ottawa is chasing is a discount, plus a procedural prize. LeBlanc says Washington has signalled that if the two sides bring the 232 and 338 tariffs down, they can begin the formal CUSMA review process written into the agreement, the one the Trump administration declined to renew in July.

## The noise around the table

Peter Navarro, Trump's trade adviser, posted a video on X on November 19 accusing Canada of cheating the United States on lumber, dairy, steel and aluminum, and calling Ottawa arrogant. BNN Bloomberg covered the remarks on Friday, and Canadian officials called them pathetic. I read that sort of thing as a negotiating position rather than a forecast, though it does tell you who believes they hold the leverage. Global News reported, citing sources, that multiple trade issues are still outstanding, with auto tariffs the core problem, which is the same issue that broke the talks in August. CBC reported there are no plans for LeBlanc to travel to Washington for in-person talks. Mark Carney has said there is progress but nothing ready to sign, and that Canada will respond to action as opposed to intent. LeBlanc has said a deal could slip to January or February.

## The cost of waiting shows up at home

Here is where the trade file stops being abstract. Statistics Canada said on November 16 that inflation held at 3.1 per cent in October, with prices excluding energy up 2.0 per cent. The unemployment rate was 6.7 per cent in October and the economy shed 4,700 jobs. GDP stalled in August. On Friday, Statistics Canada said September retail sales rose 0.8 per cent to $75.3 billion, mostly on fuel prices, and its advance estimate points to a 1.5 per cent drop in October. So we have a soft economy carrying 3.1 per cent inflation, which is the hardest combination a central bank can be handed. The Bank of Canada's policy rate is 2.5 per cent after October's increase, and the next decision lands on December 9. A tariff discount signed in February does nothing for that meeting.

## The takeaway

Watch one concrete signal, which is whether LeBlanc actually gets on a plane to Washington, because an arrangement of this size gets signed in a room. If you are in an auto-adjacent job or business, plan your first quarter assuming Section 232 tariffs are still there in some form, because LeBlanc has already said they will be. If you are renewing a mortgage before December 9, the Bank is looking at 6.7 per cent unemployment and 3.1 per cent inflation, not at a trade deal nobody can count on yet.
